claims.text: FCC high-entropy alloys show an initially pronounced stress overshoot followed by sustained strain hardening during dynamic deformation.
Lattice distortion is the primary control on the dynamic mechanical response because it impedes early dislocation nucleation and glide.
After yielding, rapid dislocation multiplication and heterogeneous dislocation interactions mitigate the transient overshoot and promote ductility.
Pre-existing dislocation networks reduce the transient flow-stress jump by partially bypassing a lattice-controlled nucleation barrier.
The annealed, as-cast baseline has a relatively low initial mobile-dislocation density.
Mild pre-straining or controlled thermomechanical processing can be used to create a controlled higher initial dislocation density for comparison with an as-cast control.
Composition-induced local lattice distortions modulate dislocation nucleation barriers, dislocation multiplication, and the spatial distribution and interactions of dislocations.
Severe lattice distortion raises the activation barrier specifically for dislocation nucleation at the onset of plasticity.
A low initial mobile-dislocation density causes marked transient behavior at the onset of plastic deformation.
Dislocation multiplication and tangling after yield produce rapid strain hardening, and sustained strain hardening supports tensile ductility.
Pre-introduced dislocations soften the initial transient response by bypassing the high nucleation barrier.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the pre-strained specimen will exhibit a reduced stress overshoot at yielding.
The pre-strained specimen will show a more gradual onset of strain hardening.
The pre-strained specimen will retain high ductility.
The pre-strained specimen may have a slightly lower overall yield strength than the as-cast baseline.
The pre-strained specimen will have a wider strain-hardening regime than the as-cast baseline.
The hypothesis applies to FCC high-entropy alloys, including the Cantor alloy, at moderate strain rates and approximately 300 K.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to BCC or amorphous high-entropy alloys.
At very high temperatures, thermal activation may alter dislocation dynamics enough to invalidate the hypothesis.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in overshoot in the higher-dislocation-density samples, or observation of essentially unchanged nucleation and hardening patterns, would falsify the proposed primary-mediator mechanism.

contradictions.description: The control state is alternately described as 'annealed, as-cast,' simply 'as-cast,' and 'as-cast (annealed).' Annealing and retaining the as-cast condition are distinct processing histories unless the intended sequence is explicitly defined.
